MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
Happy to help. Taking these in order:

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits slightly higher than the tile next to it, so the surface isn't flush. You can feel it with bare feet or catch it with a sock, and it shows up as shadows when light comes across the floor at a low angle.

It matters for your tiles in particular. Long rectangular tiles like 30 × 60 cm are often very slightly bowed in the middle. If you lay them in a half-and-half brick pattern, the high middle of one tile ends up next to the lower end of another. Most manufacturers recommend offsetting long tiles by **no more than a third** of their length. An inexpensive **tile levelling clip system** also helps a lot, and it's especially worth it for a first floor.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It hides everyday dirt, whereas white or very pale grout tends to look grubby within weeks on a floor. A colour very close to the tile gives a seamless look. A slightly darker one makes the joints look deliberate rather than dirty.

For a bathroom floor, it's also worth considering:
- a **stain-resistant or "flexible" ready-mixed grout**, or
- standard cement grout with a **grout sealer** applied after it cures.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first.** The toilet should sit on the finished tiles. That's far easier than cutting tiles around the pedestal, and it means you can replace the toilet later without damaging the floor. Just check that the soil pipe connection still lines up once the floor is a little higher.

## How many boxes

| | |
|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 × 1.8 = 4.32 m² |
| One tile | 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m² |
| Tiles needed | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = 24 |
| Plus 10% | 26.4, so **27 tiles** |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes (32 tiles)** |

**Buy 4 boxes.** Three boxes would give you exactly 24 tiles with none spare, and you will have cuts around the toilet, the door and any walls that aren't quite square. The 5 or so left over are worth keeping for future repairs, because matching a tile years later is often impossible.

Check that all the boxes have the **same batch or shade number** printed on them.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there will be some noise from about [9am] until [12pm]. We'll keep it to the morning as much as we can.
>
> Thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive these past couple of weeks. We really appreciate it, and it should be gone soon.
>
> [Your names]

A small box of biscuits through the door never hurts.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Prepare the base and dry-lay before you mix anything.** The subfloor must be solid, flat and clean. If it's timber floorboards, you'll need tile backer board or plywood over them and a flexible adhesive.

   Lay the tiles out dry first to plan where the cuts will fall. You want the full tiles where they're most visible, usually at the doorway, and no thin slivers along the edges.

2. **Get full adhesive coverage.** Use a notched trowel of about 10–12 mm for tiles this size. Comb the adhesive in straight lines and spread a thin coat on the back of each tile too ("back-buttering").

   Mix small batches so the adhesive doesn't start setting before you use it. Lift the first tile or two after pressing them down to check that the back is almost fully covered.

3. **Work towards the door and check level as you go.** Plan the order so you don't tile yourself into a corner. Check every few tiles with a spirit level or straightedge, and adjust while the adhesive is still wet.

   Then leave the floor alone. Don't walk on it or grout it for at least 24 hours, or whatever the adhesive bag says.

The videos make it look easy because the people in them have done it hundreds of times. Going slowly and checking often is exactly the right approach for a first floor. A small bathroom is a very manageable place to learn, and you're clearly preparing properly.
